title: Milton Hershey Comes Home to Lancaster After Two Failed Businesses
dek: In 1886, after candy businesses in Philadelphia and New York had failed, Milton Hershey returned home broke and started again with milk caramels.

story.event: Returning to Lancaster broke after failures in Philadelphia and New York, and starting the caramel business
story.summary: Milton Hershey's first candy business, opened in Philadelphia in 1876, went bankrupt in 1882, and a second in New York, started in 1883, failed by 1886. He returned to Lancaster, Pennsylvania, without money to ship his belongings, was shunned by most relatives, and began making milk caramels with help from a former employee, his mother and his aunt; a large British order and a bank cashier's personal guarantee turned the Lancaster Caramel Company into a success that he sold for $1 million in 1900.
paragraphs: In 1886 Milton Hershey came back to Lancaster, Pennsylvania, without the money to have his belongings shipped after him. He was not yet 30. When he walked out to his uncle's farm, the Hershey Community Archives record, most of his relatives shunned him as an irresponsible drifter. Two candy businesses had failed in ten years, and his mother's family had helped pay for them.

The first opened in Philadelphia in 1876, at 935 Spring Garden Street, a route to the Centennial Exposition. He worked such long hours that he often slept under the counter. He made too many things, candy, fruit, nuts and ice cream, and too little of any of them to profit on penny goods; the sugar dealers wanted cash while his wholesale customers expected credit and paid slowly. His uncle Abraham Snavely lent him money until he decided to stop, and in 1882, after six years, the business went bankrupt. In Denver a confectioner taught him to make caramels with fresh milk, and in 1883 he tried again in New York. That business did well at first, then ran short of cash and failed by 1886.

Back in Lancaster, Harry Lebkicher, who had worked for him in Philadelphia, stored his things and paid the shipping charges. His mother and his Aunt Mattie helped him make caramels again. Credit was the difficulty: the New York failure had left him with a bad rating, and he had little to offer as collateral beyond some cooking kettles in rented premises in a poor part of town.

Then a British candy importer placed a large order. Hershey needed a loan to buy the ingredients, and the cashier at the Lancaster County National Bank was impressed enough to back it with his own signature. When the payment arrived, the archives say, Hershey ran down the street to the bank with his apron still on. By 1890 the Lancaster Caramel Company filled its Church Street factory, and in 1900 he sold it for $1 million, keeping the chocolate business he had started inside it.

quote.text: Hence prosperous men are blockaded by troops of friends; but those who have failed stand amid vast loneliness, their friends fleeing from the very crisis which is to test their worth.
quote.work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium)
quote.locator: Letter IX, "On Philosophy and Friendship", section 9
quote.source_title: Moral letters to Lucilius, Letter 9, translated by Richard Mott Gummere (Loeb Classical Library, volume 1, 1917), Wikisource
quote.connection: Seneca describes friends who vanish when someone fails. Hershey's relatives had lent him money for years before they turned away, so the charge may be too harsh for them. Harry Lebkicher, who stored his things and paid the freight, is the friend Seneca says is rare.

reflection: It is easy to read this as a story about persistence, and it is partly that. But the record also shows how much the third attempt depended on other people: a former employee who paid the freight, a mother and an aunt at the stove, and a bank cashier who signed his own name. The relatives who refused him had their reasons too.
If something you have built falters, you find out who stays. It may be worth noticing now who already does, and thanking them before you need them, on an ordinary day rather than a desperate one.
invitation: Think of one person who helped you when your work was going badly and asked for nothing back. Send them a short note today saying what it meant, with no request attached.

sources.title: Milton Snavely Hershey in Philadelphia, 1876-1882
sources.supports: Two failed attempts before success; the shop at 935 Spring Garden Street on a route to the Centennial Exposition; long hours and sleeping under the counter; a wide range of goods including fruit, nuts and ice cream; volume too small to profit on penny goods; sugar dealers demanding cash while wholesale customers expected credit and paid slowly; Harry Lebkicher hired in 1880; repeated loans from Abraham Snavely until he decided to stop; January 1882 letter asking for a loan; bankruptcy after six years

sources.title: Milton Snavely Hershey, 1857-1945
sources.supports: Born 13 September 1857; mother's family subsidised the Philadelphia business; bankruptcy in 1882; Denver confectioner taught him caramels with fresh milk; New York business from 1883 with initial success, cash-flow problems and failure by 1886; return to Lancaster without money to ship his possessions; shunned by most relatives as an irresponsible drifter; Lebkicher stored his things and helped pay the shipping; mother and Aunt Mattie helped with production; British importer's order and the cashier backing the loan with his own signature; running to the bank in his apron; sale of the caramel company for $1 million in 1900

sources.title: Lancaster Caramel Company
sources.supports: Founded in 1886 after the New York failure; bad credit rating; little collateral beyond cooking kettles in a rented facility in a questionable part of town; the large order from a British importer and the Lancaster County National Bank cashier's personal backing; whole Church Street building occupied by 1890; Hershey Chocolate Company organised as a subsidiary in 1894; sale to the American Caramel Company on 10 August 1900 for $1 million, with the chocolate company retained

sources.title: Learning the Business
sources.supports: The Philadelphia venture's small investment, lack of equipment and staff for mass production, falling behind on bills and fear of sugar dealers cutting off supplies; the lessons about supply, credit, cash flow and limiting the product line

sources.title: Milton S. Hershey Mansion, National Register of Historic Places Inventory - Nomination Form (National Historic Landmark)
sources.supports: Independent account: Philadelphia business from 1876 at 935 Spring Garden Street, never very successful because of inadequate capital and sharp competition, closed in 1882; Denver; New York from 1883 (Sixth Avenue near Bryant Park), failed within three years; return to Lancaster in 1886 to make caramels using the fresh-milk method learnt in Denver; relatives who had bankrolled earlier ventures refusing to lend; an English importer's large order and a bank loan; sale of the caramel company in 1900 for $1 million

sources.title: The first Hershey sweets store opened in Philly
sources.supports: The 935 Spring Garden Street shop opened in 1876 and closed after six years; later ventures including New York; return to Pennsylvania and the Lancaster Caramel Company in 1886

research_notes: The slate dates the episode 1886 and names Philadelphia (1876-1882) and New York; the Hershey Community Archives and the National Park Service landmark nomination agree on 1876-1882 for Philadelphia, 1883-1886 for New York and 1886 for the return to Lancaster, so the story is told from the 1886 homecoming with the two failures as background. Where the accounts differ: the Archives say Harry Lebkicher stored Hershey's things and helped pay the shipping and that his mother and Aunt Mattie helped production, while the NPS nomination says relatives refused to lend and 'a loan from a friend' let him start, and that he peddled caramels from a pushcart; the story uses the Archives' version and does not mention the pushcart. The Archives say a bank cashier backed the loan with his own signature; the NPS says only that he obtained a bank loan. The Archives call the importer British (known only by the cable address 'DECIES'); the NPS says English. The NPS gives later Philadelphia addresses (Chestnut Street, Beech Street) that differ from the Archives' (925-927 Spring Garden Street, 532 Linden Street), so the story names only 935 Spring Garden Street, on which both agree. The NPS also mentions a short-lived Chicago venture with his father, which the Archives do not; it is left out. The $1 million sale price is the same in both. Wikipedia gives 1883 for the caramel company's start, but the Archives and NPS both say 1886. The Seneca passage is about fair-weather friendship; the connection notes that it fits Hershey's relatives only partly, since they had funded him before. The NPS PDF is a scanned form; it loads but its text layer is not read by the name check.
